title: tarski ESTree
description: The seam between the TypeScript parser bridge and the Lean evaluator: an ESTree-shaped script, narrowed to the node kinds tarski evaluates. Positions are deliberately absent — every message the evaluator produces names a node kind, never a line — and `additionalProperties` is false everywhere so a producer cannot smuggle one in. A node outside the slice is not an error here: the bridge replaces it in place with an `Unsupported` node carrying its kind, and the Lean decoder is the one place that refuses it, so there is one seam and one message.

Directive.description: A directive-prologue statement. The Lean decoder requires the script's first statement to be this node with directive "use strict", and consumes it: tarski has no sloppy mode.

VariableDeclaration.description: All three keywords are in the slice. A `var` is function-scoped and hoisted — its binding exists, holding `undefined`, before the declaration is reached — while `let` and `const` are block-scoped and have a temporal dead zone.

VariableDeclarator.description: `id` is a binding name: an Identifier or a binding pattern. A pattern with `init` `null` does not parse, and the Lean decoder refuses one as malformed.

DoWhileStatement.description: `do { … } while (…)`. The body runs before the first test, which is the whole of the difference from WhileStatement; `body` is named first here as it is in the source.

ForStatement.description: Each of the head's three parts is null when it is absent, so `for (;;)` has three. `init` is a VariableDeclaration for a declaration head and an Expression for an expression one; a head declaring a binding pattern is outside the slice and arrives as `Unsupported` in the head's place, so the loop around it still reaches the Lean decoder. `for`-`in` is ForInStatement; `for`-`of` is not this node and the whole statement arrives as `Unsupported`.

ForInStatement.description: `left` is a VariableDeclaration for a declaration head, an Expression for an assignment-target one, and an ArrayPattern or ObjectPattern for a destructuring one. The Lean decoder requires a declaration head to have exactly one declarator with no initializer: `for (var x = 1 in o)` is the sloppy-only form B.3.5 keeps alive, and it is refused by name.

ForOfStatement.description: `left` takes the same three shapes a ForInStatement's does. `await` is always false: `for await` is async iteration, which is outside the epic, and the bridge refuses the modifier in place.

LoopHead.description: The head of a `for`-`in` or a `for`-`of`: a declaration, an assignment target, or an assignment pattern.

SwitchCase.description: `test` is null for the `default` clause, which may sit anywhere among the others. `consequent` is the statements between this label and the next one: a bare list, not a block, and not a scope of its own — the whole case block is one scope.

EmptyStatement.description: The bare `;`. It completes empty, so it leaves the running completion value standing.

TryStatement.description: `try { }` with neither a handler nor a finalizer is a syntax error, so the bridge never emits one; the Lean decoder refuses such a document as malformed rather than unsupported, because no program produced it.

CatchClause.description: The optional-binding form, `catch { }`, has `param: null`. Every binding form, patterns included, is a Pattern; an out-of-slice one arrives as `Unsupported` in place, so the clause — and the `try` around it — survives.

BreakStatement.description: `label` is null for the unlabelled form. A `break` outside any loop, and a label that is not on the stack, are checker errors rather than parse errors in tsc, so they reach the evaluator: early errors are outside this epic, and such a jump escapes as the abrupt completion it is.

StringLiteral.description: A string literal, both as a directive's expression and as an ordinary value. String operations — concatenation, `length`, comparison — are a later slice; a string here can be bound, stored, compared with `===`, and produced by `typeof`.

Identifier.description: `undefined` arrives as an identifier, which is what it is in ESTree; the Lean decoder reads it as the literal a strict-mode script's non-writable global binding makes it.

UnaryExpression.description: `-`, `+`, `!`, `typeof`, `void`, and `delete` are in the slice; `~` is admitted here and refused by the Lean decoder. `delete` is not a UnaryOp in the AST — it takes a reference rather than a value — but it is a UnaryExpression here, because that is what ESTree calls it. `++` and `--` are not here — ESTree makes them an UpdateExpression, and so does this schema.

UpdateExpression.description: `++` and `--`, which ESTree separates from UnaryExpression because the side the operator sits on decides the expression's value: the prefix form answers the new number and the postfix form the old one.

BinaryExpression.description: Every ESTree binary operator, not only the slice's: the bridge writes what it saw, and the Lean decoder names the one it will not evaluate. `instanceof` and `in` are evaluated. `&&`, `||`, and `??` are not here — ESTree makes them a LogicalExpression, and so does this schema.

AssignmentExpression.description: The evaluator takes `=` and the five arithmetic compound operators — `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=` — to an identifier or a member. The schema admits every assignment operator and every target expression so that `**=`, the shifts, the bitwise and logical forms, and an out-of-slice target reach the Lean decoder and are refused there by name. A destructuring target — an ArrayPattern or an ObjectPattern — is admitted with every operator too, so that a compound one is refused there rather than here.

LogicalExpression.description: The short-circuiting operators, which ESTree separates from BinaryExpression because they do not evaluate both operands. `??` is admitted here and refused by the Lean decoder.

MemberExpression.description: `computed` says which spelling was used: `o.x` has an Identifier property and `computed: false`, `o[e]` has an arbitrary expression and `computed: true`. An optional chain (`o?.x`) is not this node — the whole access arrives as `Unsupported`. The object is `Super` for `super.x`, and the property is a `PrivateIdentifier` for `o.#x` — which is not a property key at all, but a name the class's scope resolves.

CallExpression.description: A spread argument is a SpreadElement among the `arguments`; an optional call (`f?.()`) makes the whole call `Unsupported`. A `Super` callee is `super(...)`, which runs the parent constructor rather than calling a value.

Arguments.description: An argument list, a spread in place.

NewExpression.description: `new F` without an argument list carries an empty `arguments`, as ESTree specifies.

ArrayExpression.description: A `null` element is an elision — the source's `[1, , 2]` — and a SpreadElement is `...xs`.

Property.description: One member of an object literal. `key` is an `Identifier` or a string or numeric `Literal` unless `computed`, in which case it is any expression; `value` is a `FunctionExpression` when `kind` is `"get"` or `"set"` or when `method` is true, which the Lean decoder checks. A shorthand's `value` is its own `Identifier`. Spread is a SpreadElement among the members.

TemplateElement.description: One piece of a template's text: the TV and the TRV of 12.9.6. `cooked` is null only under a tag — an escape the cooked grammar refuses is a parse error in an untagged template — and `raw` has its line terminators normalized to `\n`, as TRV requires.

TemplateLiteral.description: A template literal, tagged or not. There is one more quasi than there are expressions, so a template with no substitutions is one quasi and no expressions.

TaggedTemplateExpression.description: A tagged template. `tag` is resolved the way a call's callee is, so a member tag passes its object as `this`.

AssignmentPattern.description: A target with a default: `left` is the target and `right` the initializer, which runs only when the value is `undefined`. It is a parameter's default, an ArrayPattern element's, and an ObjectPattern property's alike.

SpreadElement.description: `...x` in an array literal, an argument list, or an object literal. In a *pattern* the same source is a RestElement instead.

RestElement.description: `...x` in a pattern: a parameter list's last parameter, an array pattern's last element, or an object pattern's last property. The Lean decoder requires it to be last and undefaulted, and refuses an object rest whose argument is itself a pattern.

ArrayPattern.description: `[a, , ...rest]` as a binding or an assignment target. A `null` element is an elision.

PatternProperty.description: One property of an ObjectPattern: a Property whose `value` is a pattern. `shorthand` is true for `{ a }` and for `{ a = 1 }`, whose `value` is then an AssignmentPattern over the same name.

ObjectPattern.description: `{ a, b: c = 1, ...rest }` as a binding or an assignment target.

Pattern.description: What a binding or an assignment pattern may be written with. A MemberExpression leaf is legal only in an *assignment* pattern; the Lean decoder is what refuses one in a binding position.

Params.description: A parameter list. Every binding form is in the slice: an Identifier, an AssignmentPattern over any pattern, an ArrayPattern or ObjectPattern, and a RestElement. A parameter property is TypeScript syntax and arrives as `Unsupported` with the modifier's kind, so the function node itself survives and only the parameter is refused.

FunctionExpression.description: `async` and `generator` are admitted here and refused by the Lean decoder: they are real syntax whose semantics are outside this epic, so the refusal names them rather than the node.

ArrowFunctionExpression.description: `expression` is true for the concise body form, whose `body` is then an Expression rather than a BlockStatement. An arrow is never a generator.

Super.description: `super`. Deliberately not an `Expression`: it may only be a member access's object or a call's callee, which are the two places above that admit it, and a `super` anywhere else does not parse.

PrivateIdentifier.description: A `#name`, with the `#` stripped as ESTree has it. Not an `Expression` either: a bare private name is legal only as the left operand of `in`, which is outside the slice, so the bridge emits `Unsupported` there and this node appears only as a member access's property.

MethodDefinition.description: A class body's constructor, method, getter, or setter. The Lean decoder refuses a private key — a private method is a non-writable element rather than a property — and a numeric key, and an `async` or generator member; the bridge emits all three so that the refusal names them rather than the class. `computed` is always false, a computed key arriving as `Unsupported` in the member's place. A `static constructor` is an ordinary static method of that name, so it arrives with `kind: "method"`.

PropertyDefinition.description: A class field. `value` is null for a field declared without an initializer, which still defines the property, holding `undefined`. A private key is in the slice here, unlike on a method.

ClassBody.description: A class body's members, in source order. A static block, a computed key, an `accessor` field, a decorator, and every TypeScript-only modifier or annotation arrive as `Unsupported` in the member's place, so the class around them still reaches the decoder. A bare `;` between members carries no meaning and is dropped.

ClassDeclaration.description: A class declaration, hoisted like a `let`: the binding exists from the top of its block and is in its dead zone until the declaration runs. An `implements` clause, a type parameter list, and a decorator each refuse the whole class rather than one member, because each says something about the class itself the slice cannot represent.

ClassExpression.description: A class expression. Its `id`, when it has one, binds the class immutably inside the class's own body and nowhere else.

Unsupported.description: A node outside the slice, standing where it appeared. `kind` is the tsc SyntaxKind name the bridge saw, and it is what the evaluator names on stderr when it refuses the script.
